source: Young, J.R. 2012. 'Biosecurity: General Principles' (Segregation, Cleaning, Disinfection), ACIAR/USYD workshop slides (mekonglivestock.wordpress.com)
text: This training material frames biosecurity as a concept rather than one fixed practice, since the right measures vary by disease, location, species, farm type, and available resources -- but underpinned everywhere by awareness of hazards (e.g. FMD, HS, CSF, HPAI) and the actual risk of occurrence in a given place and time. It sets out three key components: segregation, cleaning, and disinfection (plus vaccination and farmer behaviour as related factors). Segregation practical steps: identify physical boundaries (e.g. fencing); minimise contact between animals via tethering or feeding cut forage instead of free grazing; use fattening stalls or overnight penning; quarantine newly purchased animals separately for 2-4 weeks with daily observation; isolate sick animals, feeding/handling them last with separate equipment; observe livestock daily; only mix breeding animals with disease-free partners; avoid congregating with outside animal groups; and stay alert to local disease status. Cleaning must always happen before disinfection -- it means removing organic material (manure, soil) from shoes, clothing, vehicle tires, equipment, and hands using water, detergent, and a scrubbing brush, with wash water directed away from animals. Disinfection is then applying a chemical (or sunlight, heat, or freezing) to destroy remaining disease agents; for FMD specifically, sunlight (via drying) and acid/alkaline disinfectants at pH below 3 or above 11 are effective -- citric or hydrochloric acid at roughly 0.2% dilution, or 2% caustic soda solution, applied with basic personal protective equipment (gloves, eye protection, and always adding chemical to water, not the reverse).
